scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): agrees that research should roam beyond practical aims while granting that practical research matters too; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Some of the most useful discoveries came from research that seemed useless at the time.
One claim holds that researchers should not limit their work to areas with an immediate practical use, on the reason that the outcome of research cannot be predicted with any certainty.
I agree with both the claim and its reason, though I believe some practical research still deserves a place.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why research should roam freely

sentences.text: First, the reason behind the claim is clearly sound, since no one can predict where research will lead.
Scientists exploring pure curiosity often stumble upon discoveries far greater than any they planned.
For example, early study of electricity had no obvious use, yet it transformed the modern world.
This shows that demanding immediate usefulness would block many of our greatest breakthroughs.
Research that looks useless today may quietly become essential tomorrow.
Limiting science to the obviously practical would slowly starve discovery itself.
To this extent, the claim and its reason deserve strong support.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why practical research matters too

sentences.text: Second, however, research with an immediate practical aim also deserves real support.
Pressing problems, such as disease and hunger, demand answers that cannot simply wait.
Consider the urgent search for a vaccine during an epidemic, where practical results save lives at once.
Such work shows that aiming directly at a known problem can do enormous and immediate good.
Practical research also helps justify the public money that funds science as a whole.
A wise society supports both curious exploration and the search for immediate solutions.
Research, then, should be free to roam without abandoning practical needs entirely.
In conclusion, researchers should not be limited only to areas of obvious practical use.
But practical research still matters, since some urgent problems demand immediate answers.
The wisest approach funds free curiosity alongside the practical work that meets pressing needs.
